Welcome\! This document serves as a guide for contributing to lipu Kemeka. A glossary is available at the end. Please ask other members if you need help with anything. 

Lexicography is the field of creating dictionaries. There are many different types of dictionaries, and each individual dictionary will be tailored to suit the language or languages it is created for. Even for a single language, there may exist many different types of dictionaries. This is because dictionaries are used by all sorts of people for all sorts of reasons. 

For example, a bilingual dictionary is often used by speakers of a different language for learning or reference. A children’s dictionary may exclude complicated words and provide simplified definitions. Usually, dictionaries are made with the audience in mind, and are optimized for that audience. 

Most dictionaries are also descriptive, which means that every statement inside of them is a description of how language is used to some degree. On the contrary, linguistic prescriptivism is an instance of prescribing language usage, or how language should be used. Most dictionaries avoid this. 

What type of dictionary is lipu Kemeka? It’s an important question to answer for those who plan on contributing, so all contributors are on the same page. **lipu Kemeka is a descriptive bilingual English-to-toki pona dictionary. Its primary audience is learners who want to know the answer to “how do you say \_\_\_ in toki pona?”** All entries should serve the primary audience. So let’s talk about how to do that best. 

## 1\. How to Create a New Entry

Here is a simplified barebones version of the standard procedure for creating a new entry in lipu Kemeka. 

1. Choose your keyword  
2. Determine senses  
3. Create one row for each sense, and order them  
4. Add your name to the “submitted” column and the keyword to the “keyword” column  
5. Add parts of speech  
6. Add numbers if needed  
7. Write solution(s) in the “tok” column  
8. Write an English definition of the English word in the “eng” column  
9. Add at least one example per sense  
10. Done\! 

Here is a detailed version of the standard procedure for creating a new entry in lipu Kemeka.

1. Verify that you agree to release your contributions under CC-BY-SA-3.0 and CC-BY-SA-4.0. (A reminder is at the top of the sheet.)   
2. Choose your keyword (English word for an entry). You might have done this already. Note that entries can exist for lexicalized English phrases that are more than one word long, such as “because of” or “heart attack,” but not for English phrases like “caught the” or “fell into his” because they are not lexicalized.   
3. Determine senses (see ambiguity tests in the glossary if you need help). Make sure to check to see if there are noun, adjective, and verb senses. List them as separate rows in google sheets. You are not required to list all senses of a word.   
4. Put your name in the “submitted” column and put the English keyword in the “keyword” column, for each row of the sense. (You can also copy the code in the leftmost “time asked” column to all of your rows, but that isn’t necessary.)   
5. Assign each sense per each part of speech a number. There are two columns: one for the part of speech, and one for the enumeration. For the part of speech column, put the part of speech of the English word’s sense for that column. For the enumeration column, put the numbers in sequence, starting over at 1 when you reach a new part of speech. For meanings that are not individual senses, you may include them by putting letters (a, b, c) after the number as “subsenses.” Group senses with the same part of speech together, then order them by their frequency of usage in English (based on your knowledge). Below is the entry for “bear,” which is an exhaustive example of the procedure.   
6. Write your solution (toki pona translation of the keyword) in the “tok” column. You may put words that can be dropped in parentheses. You should list multiple solutions if you can think of them. You may include controversial and uncommon solutions, but it’s a good idea to let people know so they can discuss it.   
7. Write English definitions for each sense in the “eng” column. **Important: read this section carefully.** These must be definitions of the English words. **DO NOT** write a translation or gloss of your entry in the “tok” column. In addition, please **DO NOT** use the English word in the definition. (If you’re unsure how to write a specific definition without including the word being defined, consult wiktionary.org, Mirriam Webster, the Oxford English Dictionary, or any other monolingual English dictionary, for their entry of that word.) **DO NOT** copy English definitions from these unless their license permits it without attribution. Ask for help if you need it.   
8. Fill out example sentences. Each sense needs at least one example sentence to be displayed on the website. If you have multiple solutions listed in the “tok” column, it’s a good idea to include one example sentence for each of them. toki pona sentences must end in punctuation and must be lowercase throughout (except for proper names). English sentences must be capitalized properly, must end in punctuation, and must use punctuation where needed for clarity. Put double asterisks around the keyword and its toki pona translation.   
9. No further action is needed. 

The entry for “BEAR” is a single entry with two noun senses, two verb senses, and four subsenses.

## 2\. Usage Notes

Sometimes, listing entries is not enough, and usage notes are required for elaboration. There is a separate tab on the sheet called “Usage notes.” You may create usage notes for words you have submitted without telling anyone. It’s good practice to inform someone if you make a usage note for their submission, but that is not required either. Please make sure there is not already a usage note for a word using ctrl+f (windows) or cmnd+f (mac). If there is already a usage note, but it doesn’t describe what you wanted to include, refer to the “editing” section of this document. 

The procedure for usage notes is very simple: 

1. Put your name in the “submitted” column.  
2. Put the keyword in the “keyword” column.   
3. Put your usage note in the “notes” column.   
4. No further action is needed. 

Keep in mind:

* These usage notes will be displayed beneath all senses of the word.   
* Do not write in the first person.   
* You’re allowed to talk about silly and funny things, as long as the information is correct and useful.   
* Do not use usage notes to describe a new sense of the word. Instead, add the new sense directly to the main sheet “Definitions.”   
* You are required to be descriptive of usage. This sometimes means making clear the number of people who do or think something. You may also be descriptive of attitudes towards specific usage, but that is not required.   
* You may not be prescriptive.   
* Reach out for help if you need it. Inform other submitters if you believe your usage note is missing details or needs looking over for any reason.

Create usage notes for:

- Unique ways a solution or concept may interact with context. This includes surroundings, presuppositions (information implied by a statement), prior knowledge, and other sentences.   
- Controversy or attitudes surrounding a usage or solution. Sometimes it's a good idea to put controversial solutions in the usage notes section instead of the entry section.   
- History or details surrounding a usage or solution.   
- Methods of disambiguation between the keyword and other similar concepts, should the need arise.   
- Notes on the English keyword or a thorough breakdown of an anglophone concept, including common pitfalls of anglophone toki pona learners and how to avoid them. The pitfalls don’t have to be unique to English, i.e. there can be other languages for which these pitfalls exist. These may also include information about languages that work differently from English. Ask for help if you’re looking for examples. 

## 3\. Editing

Often, you’ll find that you need to make adjustments to submissions from other people. At this time, all contributors to lipu Kemeka are authorized to edit, as long as they follow the guidelines below. Please ask if you’re confused or need help. 

If we were to ask permission before making edits to someone else’s submission every single time we wanted something to change, the project would take longer and overwhelm most of its members, discouraging quality control. For this reason, it’s best practice to make edits and either inform the original submitter afterward, or not inform them at all. 

Whether or not you inform them may depend on the nature of your edit. Each type of edit is marked clearly below if it warrants reaching out to the original submitter, and to what degree. 

Some edits may also warrant adding your name to the “submitted” column. These are marked clearly below as well. 

These edits of entries are encouraged: 

- Spelling mistakes and grammar mistakes. Do not reach out to the original submitter.  
- Reordering senses, combining senses, and splitting senses. Do not reach out to the original submitter. You may ask for help if you’re unsure about what is and isn’t a separate sense.   
- Improvements to the English definition. Reaching out to the original submitter is not required.  
- Adding an English definition where there was no English definition. You may add your name to the “submitted” column.   
- Removal of an example sentence for being bigoted or otherwise socially problematic. Please reach out to the original submitter. If you believe the example sentence to be malicious, reach out to other members of the project instead.   
- Altering an example sentence to better fit the keyword or solution it is an example of. Reaching out to the original submitter is not required.  
- Adding a new solution (and example sentence for that solution). You may add your name to the “submitted” column.   
- Adding a new sense. Your new sense should only have your name in the “submitted” column. Do not reach out to the original submitter, as you’re the submitter now\!  
- Adding a new example sentence for someone else’s solution. This is only encouraged if there is no example sentence for that solution yet, but it is always allowed. You may add your name to the “submitted” column. 

These edits of entries are discouraged:

- Removal of an entry or sense. Reach out to the original submitter and/or other members before doing this, especially if it warrants a discussion.   
- Removal of a solution because you don’t like it or don’t think it’s effective. Reach out to other members if you believe the solution is controversial. Often, a good course of action here is to move the solution to a usage notes section so the controversy around it can be made clear to the audience of the dictionary. Often, the usage may turn out uncontroversial to most people. This always warrants discussion.   
- Removal of an example sentence because you don’t like it. You may add your own instead, but this is usually not a good enough reason to remove it.   
- Removal of a submitter’s name. If you believe there to be a mistake, reach out to other members of the project. 

These edits of usage notes are encouraged:

- Spelling and grammatical errors. Do not reach out to the original submitter.   
- Reordering paragraphs and making small changes to phrasing for the sake of flow. Do not reach out to the original submitter.   
- Adding more information. Add your name to the “submitted” column.   
- Rewording because a usage note is unclear. You may reach out to the original submitter.   
- Removing a usage note because it is bigoted or otherwise socially problematic. Please reach out to the original submitter. If you believe the usage note is malicious, reach out to other members of the project instead. 

These edits of usage notes are discouraged:

- Rewording because you dislike the phrasing, even though it is clear. In order to do this, you must reach out to the original submitter or verify that they are okay with this.   
- Removing a usage note because you don’t like it. Please do not do this. Bring it up with other members instead. 

## 4\. Glossary of Lexicography Terms

It’s important to define the terms we use in this project so contributors are not confused. Some of these terms are defined with the aid of The Dictionary of Lexicography by R. R. K. Hartman and Gregory James, and adapted to fit our project. 

**Sense** \- One general meaning of a word. For some words, like the word “cellphone,” there is only one sense: a handheld device that can be used to make calls. But for a lot of words, there is more than one sense, like the word “table,” which can refer to a surface for human usage, or the act of dropping a topic of conversation with the intent to resume it later. 

It’s important to know what meanings of a word are separate senses and what meanings aren’t, because how we present this information to our audience needs to be consistent and accurate. For example, it’s important to list the two meanings of “table” listed above as separate senses, but it would be incorrect to list “flip phone” and “smartphone” as different senses of cellphone. *See: Ambiguity Tests* for methods of testing this. 

In our dictionary, each sense is given its own row on the google sheet.

**Subsense** \- In our project, different sub-meanings of the same sense may be described as well. See the “bear” entry for a good example of this. 

**Part of Speech** \- The class a word belongs to. The classes that exist in specific languages are always based on an analysis of that language. For this project, it’s important to discuss the meaning of “Part of Speech” as it concerns English. For this project, an analysis of toki pona word classes is not necessary. 

In English, there are many parts of speech. Nouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, prepositions, pronouns, conjunctions, etc. There are a lot of these. It’s useful to include these in our project because most Anglophone readers are familiar with parts of speech. For example, “table (noun)” and “table (verb)” is often useful enough for Anglophones to tell the difference between their meanings. 

**Entry** \- Typically used to refer to a unit of a word defined. This definition for “entry” is an entry, for example. In our project, we are using one entry per English word, no matter how many senses it receives, and no matter how many parts of speech. We will still list the part of speech next to each sense because doing so makes reading the dictionary more ergonomic for our audience. 

**Ambiguity Tests** \- A test used to determine if two meanings of a word are separate senses or the same sense. This is also sometimes called “Sense Discrimination.” [The following source](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Linguistics/Analyzing_Meaning_-_An_Introduction_to_Semantics_and_Pragmatics_(Kroeger)/05%3A_Word_Senses/5.03%3A_Lexical_ambiguity) provides some of our ambiguity tests. They are described here for your convenience. 

The first test, which isn’t from the above source, is the simplest: is it possible to describe both senses with the same definition? The definition should describe both senses well and accurately. For example, “flashlight” (long tool) and “flashlight” (attachment on most smartphones) are both described well and accurately by “tool powered by electricity that shines light in one direction,” and no further nuance is needed. “Cleavage” (the space between two breasts) and “cleavage” (the act of splitting an object in half) are both things, but that definition describes neither sense well, nor accurately. Any more specific definition would fail the test, so those are separate senses. 

The second test is from the listed source. It aims to test to see if two possible meanings of a word are antagonistic. That means, can a sentence exist and refer to both meanings at the same time, or does it have to be one or the other? For example, “the thief returned home with a huge cut from his day of stealing.” “Cut” can refer to a large sum of money, or an open wound. Thieves may be likely to encounter both, but this sentence can only refer to one of these senses at a time, so they are separate and should both be listed. 

The third test is from the listed source and is called a Zuegma test. Is it possible to create a sentence where this word refers to two other words, and each of these words necessitates one of the two meanings? For example: “The door and the struggling student both needed an extra push.” For the door, “push” must be physical, but for the struggling student, “push” almost certainly refers to words of encouragement or something similar. It would be absurd to imagine someone encouraging the door to open, or someone physically applying pressure to a student who is struggling. 

The second and third methods do usually sound like jokes, and many jokes rely on lexical ambiguity in a way that can prove separate senses of a word. If in doubt, ping @lipamanka on discord. 

**Solution** \- A method to describe a concept in toki pona. The problem is, “how do you say \_\_\_ in toki pona?” The answer is the solution. There are always multiple solutions. For this project, we’re using this term because it is more accurate than “translation.”
